title: Position sizing in one formula
desc: Turn your account, risk and stop into the right number of shares

cards.title: How many shares?
cards.situation: $10,000 account, 1% risk. You buy at $50 with a stop at $48. How many shares should you buy?

options.feedback: 200 shares × $2 = $400 at risk. That’s 4% of the account, not 1%.
50 shares. If the stop is hit, you lose about $100, or 1%.
That’s the dollars lost per share, not the share count. Divide your $100 risk by it.

cards.title: One formula sets the size
cards.text: You don’t pick the [[position-size|number of shares]] by feel. The **stop** and your **risk** decide it.

visual.foot: Dollars you’ll risk ÷ dollars lost per share

blocks.tip: Find the stop first. The share count comes last.

cards.title: Size it in three steps

rows.label: Lost if the stop is hit

cards.foot: You hold $2,500 of stock, but only about $100 is at risk.

cards.title: Wider stop, fewer shares
cards.text: Same $100 risk, different stops. A **wider stop** means **fewer shares**. The risk in dollars never changes.

blocks.tip: If the share count costs more than your account, the stop is too tight or the trade is too small.

cards.title: Size the trade
cards.q: $20,000 account, 1% risk. Entry $40, stop $36. How many shares?

options.feedback: The decimal slipped. Your $200 risk ÷ $4 a share is ten times that.
$200 of risk ÷ $4 a share. If the stop is hit, you lose 1%.
That’s $400 at risk, 2% of the account. Use the full $4 gap between entry and stop.
500 shares is the whole account. A $4 drop would cost $2,000, which is 10%.

cards.title: Move the stop
cards.q: Same account, same 1% risk. You move your stop further from your entry. What happens to the number of shares?

options.feedback: It’s the other way round. Each share now loses more at the stop, so you can hold fewer.
More dollars at risk per share means fewer shares for the same dollar risk.
More dollars lost per share means fewer shares for the same dollar risk.
A wider stop costs more per share, so the count can’t go up. It shrinks.

cards.headline: You can size any trade.
lines: Set the stop first. The size comes last.
Wider stop, fewer shares. Same dollar risk.
